zone leaves free. It protects the cutback, so the back can bend without an end waiting for him.
And the H's path is misdirection: a linebacker who keys the H (follows his movement to find the play)
takes a false step the wrong way. It also builds a family. The same H motion across the formation is
the action for bootlegs and for passes to the H in the [flat](../04-the-passing-game/04-01-passing-fundamentals.qmd)
(the short area near the sideline, within a few yards of the line), so the defense cannot simply crash
on the H's path.

**What it costs.** The H is no longer available to block play-side, so the play-side is one blocker
lighter than it could be. If the defense brings an extra defender to the play-side, split zone can be
outnumbered there. Every zone variation is this kind of trade: put a blocker where the threat is,
and accept that he is not somewhere else.

## Tags: insert, arc and bash

Zone teams rarely change the line's rules. Instead they add a [tag](../01-foundations/01-04-what-a-play-really-is.qmd), a word added to the play
call that changes one or two players' jobs (you met tags in
[01-04](../01-foundations/01-04-what-a-play-really-is.qmd)). Three zone tags are worth knowing,
because you will see all three on Sundays.

```{python}
#| label: fig-zone-tags
#| fig-cap: "Two zone tags, both with inside-zone blocking to the right. Left, insert: the H (here an offset fullback) leads through the play-side B gap onto the Mike, a step ahead of the running back, so the double team on the 1 never has to climb. Right, arc: on the backside, the H (an H-back off the ball on the left) runs past the unblocked end without touching him and blocks the safety outside him. The quarterback reads that end (dashed line): if the end stays home, give; if he chases the back, keep and run behind the arc block."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.7))

# insert
off = [q for q in named_line(offense("singleback")) if q.key in (*OL_NAMES, "Y", "QB", "RB")]
off.append(Player("H", "TE", "off", -4.4, -1.8, label="H"))            # offset fullback
p = Play(off, front7(), los=35, to_go=None)
p.block("C", pts=[(1.1, 0.6)]); p.block("RG", pts=[(1.0, -0.7)])      # the double stays on the 1
p.block("RT", pts=[(0.9, 0.6)]); p.block("Y", pts=[(0.6, -0.6), (3.6, 1.5)])
p.block("LT", pts=[(0.9, 0.7)]); p.block("LG", pts=[(0.8, -0.6), (4.3, -0.8)])
go_to(p, "H", (3.7, 1.8), via=[(-2.6, 0.6), (0.3, 2.3)])                 # insert on the Mike
p.run("RB", [(3.0, 1.0), (6.0, 2.7), (10.0, 3.0)], delay=0.25)
p.highlight("H")
f = draw(p, ax=axes[0], lateral=(-7.5, 8.5), window=(-8, 6.5), title=False)
point_to(f, p, (-6.2, -4.6), (-4.4, -1.8), "H: offset\nfullback", fontsize=6.8)
point_to(f, p, (-4.2, 5.4), (0.6, 1.0), "double team\nstays on the 1", fontsize=6.8, color=ZONE_GREEN)
axes[0].set_title("Insert: H leads up on the Mike", fontsize=9, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")

# arc
off = [q for q in named_line(offense("gun_2x2")) if q.key in (*OL_NAMES, "QB")]
off += [Player("H", "TE", "off", -1.5, -6.6, label="H"), Player("RB", "RB", "off", -5.0, -1.6, label="R")]
dfn = [q for q in front7() if q.key != "SAM"] + [D("SS", "SS", 5.0, -9.6, "SS")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
p.block("C", pts=[(0.9, 0.5)]); p.block("RG", pts=[(0.8, -0.8), (4.3, -0.4)])
p.block("RT", pts=[(0.9, 0.6)])
p.block("LT", pts=[(0.9, 0.7)]); p.block("LG", pts=[(0.8, -0.6), (4.3, -0.8)])
go_to(p, "H", (4.1, -9.3), via=[(0.4, -7.6), (2.6, -9.0)])               # arc past the end to the safety
go_to(p, "RB", (1.0, 2.6), "run", via=[(-4.0, -0.4), (-1.4, 2.3)])       # give: inside zone right
p.read("BE")
p.highlight("H"); p.highlight("BE", color=style.DEFENSE)
f = draw(p, ax=axes[1], lateral=(-12, 4.0), window=(-8, 6.5), title=False)
branch(f, p, [(-5.0, 0.0), (-4.4, -2.0), (-2.6, -4.4), (-0.4, -5.4), (4.0, -6.2)], label="keep",
       label_at=(5.4, -6.0), fontsize=7, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
point_to(f, p, (-3.4, 2.8), (-1.4, 2.3), "give", fontsize=7, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
point_to(f, p, (-6.6, -9.0), (1.0, -4.0), "read end:\nnot blocked", fontsize=6.8, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
axes[1].set_title("Arc: H runs past the end", fontsize=9, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()
```

**Insert.** On [**insert**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-insert-zone-insert) (or "zone insert"),
a fullback, H-back or tight end leads up through a gap and blocks a linebacker, usually the play-side
one (some staffs insert on the backside linebacker instead). That frees the play-side double team
from having to climb: it can stay on the defensive lineman longer and move him farther. In effect,
insert adds a blocker at the point of attack, which is how a zone team answers a defense that keeps
one more defender in the [box](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd) than
the offense has blockers. The cost is the usual one: the inserting player is not available as a
receiver, and his alignment (an offset fullback, or a tight end off the ball) can tip the play.

The other two tags borrow an idea from [option football](03-04-option-football.qmd), which gets its
own chapter: instead of blocking the unblocked backside end, the quarterback *reads* him (watches
what he does after the snap) and decides whether to hand the ball off or keep it. For now, all you
need is that idea; 03-04 builds it properly.

**Arc.** Arc happens on the *backside*, away from the line's flow. The line zones right and the back
runs inside zone to the right, while on the left a tight end or H-back makes an
[**arc block**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-arc-block): he releases outside the unblocked
backside end, runs past him without touching him, and blocks the *next* defender out, the linebacker or
safety responsible for the alley between the end and the sideline (the
[alley player](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-05-run-fits-and-box-math.qmd) of Part 5). The
quarterback reads the end. If the end stays home, the quarterback gives and the back runs inside zone.
If the end chases the running back down the line, the quarterback keeps, runs around the end the other
way, and finds the arc block already waiting for the next man. Arc is why you sometimes see a tight end
run right past a defensive end without touching him: he was never supposed to.

Bash needs one more step of background. On the standard **zone read** (03-04 draws it), the back runs
the inside-zone track and the quarterback, reading the backside end, keeps the ball around that end if
the end chases the back. Defenses learned an answer: the end crashes down hard at the back, inviting the
keep, while a linebacker loops around behind him to meet the quarterback where he was about to run (a
**scrape exchange**: the end and the linebacker swap jobs).[^scrape] The defense's plan is a bet that the
back will be inside and the quarterback outside.

```{python}
#| label: fig-zone-bash
#| fig-cap: "The zone read and bash, both with the line zoning right and the quarterback reading the same backside end (dashed line). Left, the zone read: the back takes the inside-zone track, and the quarterback keeps around the end if the end chases the back. Right, bash: the back goes the other way, wide around the end, and the quarterback, if he keeps, runs the inside-zone track. The runners have swapped lanes, so a defense planning for 'back inside, quarterback outside' has it backwards."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.5))
for ax, bash in [(axes[0], False), (axes[1], True)]:
    off = [q for q in named_line(offense("gun_2x2")) if q.key in (*OL_NAMES, "QB")]
    off += [Player("RB", "RB", "off", -5.0, 1.6 if bash else -1.6, label="R"),
            Player("Y", "TE", "off", -0.7, 4.8, label="Y")]
    p = Play(off, front7(), los=35, to_go=None)
    p.block("C", pts=[(0.9, 0.5)]); p.block("RG", pts=[(0.8, -0.8), (4.3, -0.4)])
    p.block("RT", pts=[(0.9, 0.6)]); p.block("Y", pts=[(0.6, -0.6), (3.6, 1.5)])
    p.block("LT", pts=[(0.9, 0.7)]); p.block("LG", pts=[(0.8, -0.6), (4.3, -0.8)])
    p.read("BE")
    p.highlight("BE", color=style.DEFENSE)
    f = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-9.5, 7.0), window=(-8, 7), title=False)
    inside = [(-5.0, 0.0), (-3.6, 1.0), (-1.2, 2.3), (4.6, 2.7)]
    outside = [(-4.6, -1.0), (-3.6, -3.4), (-1.6, -6.2), (3.6, -7.6)]
    if bash:
        branch(f, p, [(-5.0, 1.6), (-4.8, 0.4)] + outside, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK,
               label="give (back)\nif the end squeezes", label_at=(-6.6, -5.6), fontsize=6.6)
        branch(f, p, inside, color=ZONE_GREEN, label="keep (QB) if the end\nwidens with the back",
               label_at=(6.2, 3.0), fontsize=6.6)
        ax.set_title("Bash: back outside, QB inside", fontsize=9, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
    else:
        branch(f, p, [(-5.0, -1.6), (-3.8, 0.0)] + inside[2:], color=style.OFFENSE_DARK,
               label="give (back)", label_at=(6.0, 3.2), fontsize=6.6)
        branch(f, p, [(-5.0, 0.0)] + outside, color=ZONE_GREEN, label="keep (QB) if the\nend chases the back",
               label_at=(-6.6, -5.6), fontsize=6.6)
        ax.set_title("Zone read: back inside, QB outside", fontsize=9, loc="left", color=style.INK,
                     fontweight="bold")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()
```

**Bash.** [**Bash**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-bash) is short for "back away": the running
back runs *away* from the direction the line is zoning, on a wide path around the read end, while
the quarterback, if he keeps, runs the inside-zone track behind the line (@fig-zone-bash). It flips
the usual roles: the running back threatens the edge and the quarterback becomes the inside runner.
The read is the same end, with the answers reversed: if he *squeezes* (closes down the line toward
the zone flow), the quarterback hands the ball to the back going around him; if he stays wide to take
the back, the quarterback keeps and runs inside him.[^bash] Against a scrape exchange, that matters: the
end who crashes down to take the inside runner has crashed onto the quarterback's fake, and the ball is
going outside him with the running back. Bash is the offense's reply to the defense's reply, and the full
back-and-forth belongs to [option football](03-04-option-football.qmd).

All three tags share one logic: **keep the zone rules for the line, and change one or two players
to fix the specific problem the defense is creating.** Watch for the extra player (the inserting
back, the arcing tight end, the back running the "wrong" way) and you will usually know which tag you
are watching.

## How defenses fight zone

Zone's rules guarantee that every defender is accounted for. They do not guarantee that every block is
won, and defenses attack the places where zone is physically hardest. @fig-zone-defense shows the two
most common.

```{python}
#| label: fig-zone-defense
#| fig-cap: "Two ways defenses kill outside zone right. Left: penetration. This time the 3-technique lines up on the play side; at the snap he knifes upfield through the B gap, before the lateral-stepping guard and tackle can get in front of him, and meets the back on his track. Right: a cutback player. Instead of flowing, the Will comes downhill into the backside A gap at the snap, faster than the left guard can climb to him, so when the back bends, the lane he expected is filled."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.6))
# penetration: the 3-technique lines up on the play side this time (Sam still on the right)
dfn = [D("PE", "DE", 1.0, technique("5", 1), "5"), D("PT", "DT", 1.0, technique("3", 1), "3"),
       D("BT", "DT", 1.0, technique("1", -1), "1"), D("BE", "DE", 1.0, technique("5", -1), "5"),
       D("SAM", "SAM", 4.0, 6.6, "S"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 0.6, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -3.0, "W")]
off = [q for q in ace_condensed() if q.key not in ("X", "Z")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
for k, st in [("LT", (0.1, 1.3)), ("LG", (0.1, 1.3)), ("C", (0.1, 1.2)), ("U", (0.1, 1.3)), ("Y", (0.2, 0.9))]:
    p.block(k, pts=[st])
p.block("RG", pts=[(-0.1, 1.1)]); p.block("RT", pts=[(0.0, 0.9)])
go_to(p, "PT", (-2.7, 3.0), "path")                       # the play-side 3-technique penetrates
go_to(p, "RB", (-2.8, 3.4), "run", via=[(-4.4, 2.4)])
go_to(p, "QB", (-3.6, 1.8), "path", speed=3.2)
p.highlight("PT", color=style.DEFENSE)
f = draw(p, ax=axes[0], lateral=(-7.5, 8.5), window=(-8, 6.5), title=False)
x, y = _P(f, p, -2.9, 3.5)
axes[0].plot([x], [y], marker="X", ms=11, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, mec="white", mew=0.8, zorder=12)
say(f, p, -2.4, 6.4, "tackle\nfor loss", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
point_to(f, p, (-5.8, 6.0), (1.0, 2.35), "3-tech knifes upfield\nbefore the reach", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK,
         fontsize=6.8)
axes[0].set_title("Penetration", fontsize=9, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")

# cutback player: the Will plays fast into the backside A gap before the LG can climb to him
# (the quarterback is left out of this panel so the bend lane behind the line stays visible)
p = Play([q for q in off if q.key != "QB"], front7(+1), los=35, to_go=None)
for k in ("LT", "C", "RG", "RT", "U", "Y"):
    p.block(k, pts=[(0.15, 1.3)])
go_to(p, "LG", (1.4, -0.3), via=[(-0.3, -0.9)])            # steps play-side to climb: late
go_to(p, "MIKE", (3.6, 4.6), "path"); go_to(p, "SAM", (3.4, 8.0), "path")
go_to(p, "WILL", (1.0, -1.1), "path", speed=4.0)           # downhill into the backside A gap
go_to(p, "RB", (-1.9, 4.8), "run", via=[(-4.4, 2.4)])
p.highlight("WILL", color=style.DEFENSE)
f = draw(p, ax=axes[1], lateral=(-7.5, 8.5), window=(-8, 6.5), title=False)
branch(f, p, [(-1.9, 4.8), (-2.1, 2.4), (-1.8, 0.2), (-0.6, -0.6), (-0.1, -0.75)], color=style.OFFENSE_DARK,
       label="bend", label_at=(-3.2, 0.6), fontsize=7)
x, y = _P(f, p, 0.25, -0.85)
axes[1].plot([x], [y], marker="X", ms=11, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, mec="white", mew=0.8, zorder=12)
point_to(f, p, (-5.0, -4.6), (1.0, -1.1), "Will plays fast into\nthe backside A gap,\nbefore the LG can climb",
         color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
axes[1].set_title("The cutback player", fontsize=9, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()
```

**Penetration and movement.** A defensive lineman who gets upfield at the snap, or slants hard toward
the play, can beat a lateral-stepping blocker to the spot. Defenses that want to stop zone often play
their linemen this way, attacking a gap instead of reading the man in front of them; how defensive
linemen are taught to do either is the subject of
[05-01](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-01-dl-techniques-and-gap-control.qmd).

**The cutback player.** Because outside zone's biggest gains come from the cutback, defenses assign
someone to stay home for it: usually the backside linebacker, sometimes a safety rotating down. You
saw the deep safety arrive late in @fig-cutback; a defense that gets a defender there *early* takes away
the play's third answer.

**Spill or squeeze.** When a blocker comes at a defender, the defense chooses whether that defender
fights *inside* the block to force the ball to bounce wide toward pursuit (*spill*) or holds the edge
and squeezes the play back inside (*squeeze*). Against zone, either plan can work if all eleven
players agree on it, which is the subject of run fits in
[05-05](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-05-run-fits-and-box-math.qmd).[^fits]

And when the defense simply puts more defenders in the box than the offense has blockers, a zone team
answers with the tools you have already seen: an extra blocker (insert), a read of the unblocked man
(arc, bash, the zone read), or a pass that looks like the run.

## Why wide zone and the bootleg are married

Outside zone's greatest weapon is not a run at all. It is the pass that looks exactly like it.

Think about what outside zone teaches a defense. Every snap, the line steps hard to one side, the
back runs at the tight end, and the linebackers learn that if they do not flow fast and hard, they
lose. The backside end learns that if he does not chase, the cutback beats him. After a few of
these, the defense is *trained* to run with the line's first step.

The [bootleg](../04-the-passing-game/04-05-play-action-boots-screens.qmd) cashes that in. It is a
[play-action](../04-the-passing-game/04-05-play-action-boots-screens.qmd) pass (a pass that begins
with a fake handoff) in which the quarterback fakes outside zone one way and rolls out the other,
away from where the line went, with receivers crossing the field to meet him. In the "naked" version
nobody blocks for him at all; in the protected version a lineman or a back is assigned to the backside
end. Both are built in [04-05](../04-the-passing-game/04-05-play-action-boots-screens.qmd); here, what
matters is why they pair with zone.

```{python}
#| label: fig-zone-boot
#| fig-cap: "The same first second. Left: outside zone right; the U cuts off the backside end. Right: a naked bootleg left off the same look. The line's first steps, the back's track and the linebackers' flow are identical (grey note). What differs: on the boot, nobody blocks the backside end; if he chases the fake down the line onto the back's track, he ends up behind a quarterback rolling away from him, who has three receivers at three depths on the boot side: the U in the flat, the Y on a crossing route (releasing inside the play-side end) and the Z on a deep over route."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 4.3))
for i, ax in enumerate(axes):
    p = Play(ace_condensed(), even_front(+1, cb_w=10.0), los=35, to_go=10)
    for k in ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT"):
        p.block(k, pts=[(0.15, 1.4)])                      # identical first steps
    go_to(p, "MIKE", (4.3, 4.4), "path"); go_to(p, "WILL", (4.3, 1.2), "path")
    go_to(p, "SAM", (3.8, 8.2), "path")
    if i == 0:
        go_to(p, "U", (0.4, -3.4), via=[(-0.5, -4.2)])     # cut off the end
        go_to(p, "BE", (1.0, -3.0), "path")
        go_to(p, "Y", (0.3, 5.9))
        go_to(p, "QB", (-3.6, 1.8), "path", speed=3.2)
        go_to(p, "RB", (2.5, 5.0), "run", via=[(-4.3, 2.6), (-1.3, 4.9)])
        p.route("X", [(0, 0), (9, 0)]); go_to(p, "Z", (4.0, 9.8))
        p.highlight("RB")
        f = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-13, 12), window=(-9, 17.5), title=False)
        ax.set_title("Outside zone right", fontsize=9, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
    else:
        go_to(p, "BE", (-2.2, 2.6), "path", via=[(0.4, -3.6), (-1.75, -2.6), (-2.0, 0.0)])  # chases the fake
        go_to(p, "QB", (-3.4, 1.6), "path", speed=3.2)                  # the same fake ...
        go_to(p, "QB", (-6.0, -7.5), "path", speed=4.5, delay=0.1)      # ... then roll the other way
        go_to(p, "RB", (1.0, 5.6), "path", via=[(-4.3, 2.6), (-1.3, 4.9)])
        p.route("U", [(0, 0), (1.5, 1.0), (4.5, 7.5)], delay=0.6)       # flat, boot side
        p.route("Y", [(0, 0), (1.2, -1.0), (4.5, -4.0), (7.0, -8.0), (7.5, -12.5)])  # inside the 5, then across
        p.route("X", [(0, 0), (14, 0.5)])                               # clear out
        p.route("Z", [(0, 0), (10, -1.0), (15, -10), (16, -17)])         # deep over, all the way across
        p.highlight("QB")
        f = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-13, 12), window=(-9, 17.5), title=False)
        say(f, p, 2.4, -10.6, "flat", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
        say(f, p, 8.6, -5.0, "cross", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
        say(f, p, 16.2, -3.0, "over", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
        point_to(f, p, (-7.6, 6.0), (-1.9, 0.6), "end chases\nthe fake", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
        ax.set_title("Naked boot left, same first second", fontsize=9, loc="left", color=style.INK,
                     fontweight="bold")
    if i == 0:
        say(f, p, -6.8, -7.6, "first steps and linebacker\nflow: the same in both", color=style.MUTED, fontsize=6.6)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.5)
plt.show()
```

The two plays look identical for the first second, which is the second that decides how the
defense moves. (The "over" route is a deep crossing route: the receiver runs across the field 15 or
more yards downfield, *over* the linebackers.) On a bootleg the backside end's job is to *contain* the quarterback: stay outside him
and force him back toward the pursuit. An end who chased the run fake (as outside zone has taught him
to) is now *behind* a quarterback rolling away from him, and nobody is there to make the quarterback
hurry. The linebackers who flowed with the line are a step or two the wrong way, and the
*crossing routes* (receivers running across the field) come open behind them. The boot gives the
quarterback three receivers at three depths on the same side: a short one in the flat, one crossing
at linebacker depth, and one deep. That simple read is what makes the play so reliable.

**Why the pair works.** Each play protects the other. If the defense sits back and refuses to flow,
outside zone gets the edge or the crease. If it flows hard, the bootleg punishes the flow. And because
the two share the same first step, the defense cannot wait to find out which one it is facing. This
is the backbone of the Shanahan-family offenses you will meet in
[12-03](../12-case-studies/12-03-shanahan-wide-zone-tree.qmd): a run game and a play-action game built
to be indistinguishable for as long as possible.

**How to tell them apart after the snap.** Three plays send a tight end or H-back at the backside
end, and before the snap they can look the same. Watch what he does when he gets there:

- He **hits** the end and drives him out: split zone.
- He runs **past** the end without touching him and blocks the *next* man out (a linebacker or safety),
  while the quarterback rides the ball with the back and watches the end: arc.
- He runs past the end into the flat and **turns to look for the ball**, while the quarterback pulls the
  ball and rolls the other way: bootleg.

**The cost.** A naked bootleg leaves the quarterback with nobody blocking the backside end. If that end
does *not* bite on the fake (if he stays home), he is waiting for a quarterback who has turned his back
to him. That is why the bootleg works only once outside zone has earned the defense's respect.

## Where zone came from

Running backs reading blocks is as old as football. Vince Lombardi's Green Bay Packers of the 1960s
ran their famous power sweep with a simple instruction to the ball carrier: run to daylight, wherever
the blocks open it, a phrase that became the title of a 1963 book Lombardi wrote with W. C.
Heinz.[^lombardi] That sweep was a gap play with pulling guards, not a zone play, but its runner's
freedom to choose the hole is the same idea zone backs live by.

Who invented zone *blocking* is disputed, and nobody serious claims a single inventor. The best-documented
claims put it in the NFL of the 1980s. Jim McNally, the Cincinnati Bengals' offensive line coach, was
one of the era's most copied line coaches, and Cincinnati's run game finished in the league's top five
every year from 1986 to 1990. McNally himself said, "I didn't invent zone blocking, but we and the
Cleveland Browns did it back in the '80s," and he described it as an answer to the rise of the 3-4
defense and its penetrating linemen. Cleveland's line coach in those years was Howard Mudd,
the same coach who later made the stretch a Colts signature.[^origins] Coaches who credit older roots
point to blocking ideas in earlier college offenses; treat any one-name "inventor" story with suspicion.

What is not in dispute is who made outside zone the identity of an NFL offense. **Alex Gibbs**, an
offensive line coach with a famously blunt teaching style and a reputation as one of the best line
coaches of his era, built the Denver Broncos' running game under head coach **Mike Shanahan** from
1995.[^gibbs] Denver had a specific problem to solve. Pittsburgh defensive coordinator Dom Capers had
popularized the *zone blitz*, in which a linebacker blitzes and a lineman drops into coverage in his
place, so the defenders a man-blocking line had assigned itself kept changing. "When you're in a man
scheme, you're getting picked off and you look bad," Gary Kubiak, then Denver's offensive coordinator,
later remembered.[^espn2019] (In blocking, "picked off" means a blocker's path is cut off by a defender
he was not assigned, so his own man runs free: exactly the left side of @fig-zone-vs-movement.) Blocking by area meant that whoever came was blocked.

Gibbs's system was close to a religion: a small number of runs, repeated until the linemen could
execute them against any front; light, quick linemen who could reach and run; backside cut blocks; and
backs taught to press the aiming point and make one cut. His clinic tapes on zone running circulated
widely among coaches and are still sold as coaching videos, and many of the phrases in this chapter
descend from his teaching.[^gibbstapes]

Denver's results became the advertisement. The Broncos won back-to-back Super Bowls after the 1997 and
1998 seasons, and running back Terrell Davis, a sixth-round draft pick, ran for 2,008 yards in 1998
and was named the league's MVP.[^davis] When injuries ended Davis's peak, Denver kept producing
1,000-yard rushers with a string of other backs, several of them mid- or late-round picks, which
convinced the league that the *scheme* was doing much of the work.[^denverbacks]

The system spread through a coaching tree. Gary Kubiak carried it to Houston as head coach and back to
Denver, where he won Super Bowl 50 after the 2015 season. Kyle Shanahan, Mike's son, coached under
Kubiak in Houston and under his father in Washington, then became the 49ers' head coach in 2017. From
Kyle Shanahan's staffs came Sean McVay (Rams), Matt LaFleur (Packers) and others, and Kubiak's son Klint
called plays for the 2025 Seattle Seahawks before becoming the Raiders' head coach for 2026.[^tree] By
late in the 2019 season, ESPN's charting found zone blocking in use by all 32 teams and on at least half
of the runs of most of them; LaFleur's Packers led the league at 70.3% of runs (same ESPN study). The tree and its
offense get a full case study in [12-03](../12-case-studies/12-03-shanahan-wide-zone-tree.qmd).

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Denver Broncos, Super Bowl XXXII (1997 season)"}
**The game:** Super Bowl XXXII, January 25, 1998: Denver 31, Green Bay 24. Terrell Davis carried 30
times for 157 yards and three touchdowns and was named MVP, despite a migraine that blurred his vision
and kept him out of part of the second quarter.[^sb32] Coaches' film from the 1990s is hard to find, but
Super Bowl broadcasts are the easiest games of the era to track down, and this one is dominated by Gibbs's
zone running (Denver mixed in other runs and play-action too).

**What to notice:**

- The line's first step. Every lineman moves laterally together; you will seldom see a Denver guard pull.
- Davis's patience. He runs at the tight end's outside leg for two or three steps and does not cut until
  the end commits. Then he cuts once, hard, and is going north.
- The backside. Watch the defensive linemen away from the play. Many end up on the ground in the first
  second: that is the backside cut, and it is why Davis's cutbacks so often had nobody in them.
- The bootleg. John Elway faking the stretch and rolling away is the other half of the same system.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: San Francisco 49ers 2019"}
**The game:** the NFC Championship Game after the 2019 season, 49ers vs. Green Bay Packers, January 19,
2020. San Francisco won 37–20 and threw the ball only eight times; running back Raheem Mostert, a
former undrafted free agent, ran for 220 yards and four touchdowns.[^mostert]

**What to notice:**

- How often the 49ers ran the wide-zone family, and how little they disguised it. They were not a pure
  zone team (the same ESPN charting had them using zone on 55% of their runs that season), so gap runs and
  tosses came off the same formations. Make it a drill: classify each run with this chapter's
  Watch-for-it checklist (does the whole line step together, or does a guard pull?).
- The linebackers. As the game goes on, watch them flow harder and harder to the play-side, and watch the
  cutbacks and the inside creases that opens.
- Mostert's runs: many of his biggest gains come on one cut, at full speed, into a crease that appeared
  only after the defense flowed.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Seattle Seahawks, Super Bowl LX (2025 season)"}
**The game:** Super Bowl LX, February 8, 2026: Seattle 29, New England 13, the end of Klint Kubiak's single
season as Seattle's offensive coordinator (he became the Raiders' head coach for 2026, so this is one season's
offense, not Seattle's current one). Running back Kenneth Walker III carried 27 times for 135 yards and was
named MVP.[^lx] Kubiak's offense descends directly from the Gibbs-Shanahan-Kubiak tree, built on outside zone
from tight, two-tight-end formations and the bootlegs that pair with it.[^sea]

**What to do:** watch Walker's 27 carries with this chapter's checklist. For each one, call it zone or gap
(does the whole line step together?), inside or outside (up or across?), and bang, bend or bounce. Then count
the bootlegs and play-action passes that started with the same first step. It is the 2019 49ers' film, a
quarter-century after Denver.
:::

One more modern example worth finding: Christian McCaffrey's 2023 season in San Francisco, when he led
the NFL with 1,459 rushing yards and was named Offensive Player of the Year.[^cmc] He is not a pure
one-cut back (he will press, hop sideways and cut again), which makes him a good contrast with Davis and
Mostert: watch how he uses the same aiming points with a different running style.

## Does it work? Reading the numbers

You might expect a data source to tell us how well zone runs work. It cannot, directly, and the reason
is worth understanding before looking at any chart.

The NFL's play-by-play data (which nflverse packages for free) records *where* a run went, not what
play was called. Each run gets a **run location** (left, middle or right) and, unless it went up the
middle, a **run gap** (guard, tackle or end). These are charted by the league's scorers from where the
ball carrier crossed the line, and they are coarser than the gap letters of 03-01: roughly, "middle" is
between the guards (the A gaps), "guard" is over or just outside a guard (the B gap), "tackle" is over or
just outside a tackle (the C gap), and "end" is outside the last man on the line. There is no "zone" flag. So a zone run that cuts back is logged where the
back ended up, not where the play was aimed. (Commercial charting services such as PFF, Pro Football
Focus, do label run concepts by watching film. In the sample of their labels released with the 2025
Big Data Bowl (2022 season), outside zone was the single most common run concept.[^bdbcol] That is the most
recent public count we know of; no league-wide zone share for 2025 has been published that we could check.)

So to study zone we need a proxy: a team we know runs a lot of zone. We use Kyle Shanahan's 49ers. LaFleur's
Packers ran an even higher share of zone in ESPN's 2019 count, and would also do; the 49ers are the root of the
coaching tree and the subject of the [12-03](../12-case-studies/12-03-shanahan-wide-zone-tree.qmd) case study,
and Shanahan was their head coach for every season in the chart. (The Packers' number appears below too.)

One more thing before the chart: **expect negative numbers.** Across the league, the average running-back
carry *loses* a little expected value, because a typical run gains less than the down and distance needs to
keep the offense's scoring chances where they were. So "good" on this chart means "less negative than the
league," and a run game is judged by how far above the league line it sits, not by whether it clears zero.

With those caveats, here is the 49ers' efficiency by run location against the league average from 2019 to
2025. The measures are [EPA per rush](../01-foundations/01-02-downs-distance-and-field-position.qmd) (how
much each run changed the offense's expected points, on average; above zero is good for the offense) and
[success rate](../01-foundations/01-02-downs-distance-and-field-position.qmd) (the share of runs with
positive EPA). Only running back and fullback carries count, so quarterback runs and receivers' jet
sweeps and end-arounds, which are not zone runs, stay out.

```{python}
#| label: fig-epa-by-location
#| fig-cap: "Rushing efficiency by run location, 49ers vs. the league, 2019-2025 regular seasons (running back and fullback carries only; runs pooled across left and right). Nearly every value is below zero: the average carry loses a little expected value. Runs to the end look best for everyone, partly by selection (explained below). The 49ers beat the league average in every lane, by small margins. Note the success-rate axis starts at 30%, so its gaps look bigger than they are. Data: nflverse play-by-play and rosters via nflreadpy."
from gridiron.data import pbp, nfl

style.apply()
SEASONS = list(range(2019, 2026))
cols = ["season", "season_type", "posteam", "play_type", "run_location", "run_gap", "epa",
        "success", "qb_scramble", "qb_kneel", "down", "rusher_player_id"]
plays = pbp(SEASONS, columns=cols)
rosters = nfl().load_rosters(SEASONS).to_pandas()
back_ids = set(rosters.loc[rosters["position"].isin(["RB", "FB"]), "gsis_id"].dropna())

runs = plays[(plays["season_type"] == "REG") & (plays["play_type"] == "run")
             & (plays["qb_scramble"] == 0) & (plays["qb_kneel"] == 0)
             & plays["epa"].notna() & plays["down"].notna() & plays["run_location"].notna()
             & plays["rusher_player_id"].isin(back_ids)].copy()
runs["lane"] = np.where(runs["run_location"] == "middle", "Middle", runs["run_gap"].str.title())
runs = runs[runs["lane"].isin(["Middle", "Guard", "Tackle", "End"])]
LANES = ["Middle", "Guard", "Tackle", "End"]

def by_lane(df):
    return df.groupby("lane").agg(n=("epa", "size"), epa=("epa", "mean"),
                                  sr=("success", "mean")).reindex(LANES)

lg, sf = by_lane(runs), by_lane(runs[runs["posteam"] == "SF"])
gap = sf["epa"] - lg["epa"]
team = runs.groupby("posteam")["epa"].mean().sort_values(ascending=False)
sf_rank = list(team.index).index("SF") + 1
gb_rank, gb_all = list(team.index).index("GB") + 1, team["GB"]
n_pos = int((team > 0).sum())
lg_all, sf_all = runs["epa"].mean(), runs.loc[runs["posteam"] == "SF", "epa"].mean()
ordinal = lambda n: f"{n}{'th' if 10 <= n % 100 <= 20 else {1: 'st', 2: 'nd', 3: 'rd'}.get(n % 10, 'th')}"
pct = lambda v: f"{100 * v:.0f}%"

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.3))
x = np.arange(len(LANES))
for ax, col, ttl, fmt in [(axes[0], "epa", "EPA per rush", "{:+.2f}"),
                          (axes[1], "sr", "Success rate (axis from 30%)", "{:.0%}")]:
    for frame, name, color in [(sf, "49ers", style.SERIES[0]), (lg, "League", style.SERIES[1])]:
        ax.plot(x, frame[col], color=color, lw=2, marker="o", ms=7, mec=style.SURFACE, mew=1.5,
                label=name, zorder=3)
        ax.annotate(f"{name} {fmt.format(frame[col].iloc[-1])}", (x[-1], frame[col].iloc[-1]),
                    xytext=(7, 0), textcoords="offset points", va="center", fontsize=7.5, color=style.INK_2)
    if col == "epa":
        ax.axhline(0, color=style.BASELINE, lw=1, zorder=1)
    else:
        ax.set_ylim(0.30, 0.48)
    ax.set_xticks(x, [f"{l}\n{lg.loc[l, 'n'] / 1000:.1f}k" for l in LANES], fontsize=7.5)
    ax.set_xlim(-0.3, 4.1)
    ax.set_title(ttl, fontsize=10)
    ax.tick_params(axis="y", labelsize=7.5)
    ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
axes[1].yaxis.set_major_formatter(plt.FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: f"{v:.0%}"))
axes[0].legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=7.5)
fig.supxlabel("Where the run went, from the middle out (league carries in each lane)", fontsize=8, color=style.INK_2)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Four things to read from @fig-epa-by-location.

**Runs that reach the end are the least bad, for everyone.** League-wide, running back carries logged
at the end averaged `{python} f"{lg.loc['End', 'epa']:+.3f}"` EPA per rush, against
`{python} f"{lg.loc['Middle', 'epa']:+.3f}"` up the middle. That does *not* mean "always run outside." It
means that when a run gets outside, it is usually because the edge was open, and the runs that tried to get
outside and failed were often logged somewhere else (or as losses at the tackle). This is a **selection
effect** (backs only go outside when the edge is open, so the runs that get there are the lucky ones), and it
is why no coordinator reads this chart as a play-calling instruction.

**The 49ers were a little better everywhere, most of all at the two ends of the chart.** Their EPA edge
over the league was `{python} f"{gap['End']:+.3f}"` per carry at the end and
`{python} f"{gap['Middle']:+.3f}"` up the middle, against `{python} f"{gap['Guard']:+.3f}"` at guard and
`{python} f"{gap['Tackle']:+.3f}"` at tackle. That fits outside zone's two big answers, the bounce (logged at
the end) and the cutback (often logged up the middle), but the gaps are small, a few hundredths of a point
per carry, and the chart cannot prove the scheme caused them.

**Success rate tells a slightly different story.** San Francisco's success rate beat the league's by
`{python} f"{100 * (sf.loc['Guard', 'sr'] - lg.loc['Guard', 'sr']):.1f}"` points at guard and
`{python} f"{100 * (sf.loc['Middle', 'sr'] - lg.loc['Middle', 'sr']):.1f}"` up the middle, but only
`{python} f"{100 * (sf.loc['Tackle', 'sr'] - lg.loc['Tackle', 'sr']):.1f}"` at tackle. Success rate rewards
steady, positive gains; EPA also rewards big ones. A team can be consistent inside and explosive outside,
and the two panels let you see both.

**Overall, good, not magic.** Across all seven seasons the 49ers' running back carries averaged
`{python} f"{sf_all:+.3f}"` EPA per rush against a league average of `{python} f"{lg_all:+.3f}"`, ranking
`{python} ordinal(sf_rank)` of 32 teams; `{python} ("only one team" if n_pos == 1 else f"only {n_pos} teams" if n_pos else "no team")`
averaged above zero. LaFleur's Packers, the other famous zone offense of the period, averaged
`{python} f"{gb_all:+.3f}"` and ranked `{python} ordinal(gb_rank)`. So two of the period's best-known zone
offenses landed in quite different places, `{python} "both above the league average" if min(sf_all, gb_all) > lg_all else "and not both above the league average"`.
That spread is the lesson: zone is one input to a run game, alongside the backs, the linemen, the quarterback and
what the passing game makes defenses fear. Part of the 49ers'
edge is surely talent rather than scheme (McCaffrey, the 2023 Offensive Player of the Year, carried for them),
and run-location data cannot separate the two; that would take play-level scheme labels and a model of
player quality. Teams still run, even though the average carry loses a little expected value, because a run
game does things a single carry's EPA does not
capture: it keeps the defense honest, it shortens third downs, and above all it sets up the play-action
passes that look like it. You will see that argument tested with data in
[13-02](../13-analytics-and-data/13-02-expected-points-and-success-rate.qmd).

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"Run location tells you which runs a team called." It tells you where the ball carrier went. On zone runs
especially, those are different things: an outside zone that cuts back is logged up the middle. Treat
run-location splits as a picture of *outcomes*, and be suspicious of anyone who ranks "best run plays"
from them.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it"}
**On Sunday: bang, bend, bounce.** You cannot watch everything in two seconds, so watch in this order.

*Before the snap* (you have time here)

- Count the tight ends and find the running back. Two tight ends and a back directly behind the quarterback
  (or in the pistol) is a natural zone look. In the shotgun, an inside-zone back usually runs *away* from the
  side he lines up on, crossing the quarterback's face. (How deep the back stands varies too much by team to
  be a reliable tell on its own.)
- Find the backside end, the defender farthest from where you think the play is going. Remember where he is;
  you will check on him after the play.

*The first half-second: watch the line, nothing else*

- Do all five linemen step the same way? Zone. Does a guard pull? Gap scheme
  ([03-03](03-03-gap-and-power-runs.qmd)). Double teams but no zone steps, and the back aiming straight at a
  linebacker? Probably duo, also in 03-03.
- Are the linemen's helmets going *up* (inside zone) or *across* (outside zone)? The high end-zone replay angle
  shows this best (01-06); on the live sideline angle, look for the whole line drifting toward one sideline.

*Then: watch the back's feet*

- Where is he aiming: the guard, or the tight end? Wider than the tight end is stretch.
- Watch him press, plant and cut. Call it as it happens: **bang** (play-side gaps), **bend** (back against the
  flow) or **bounce** (outside the end).

*After the play (on the replay)*

- Did a tight end or H-back go at the backside end? Hit him: split zone. Ran past him to the next man: arc.
  Slipped into the flat looking for the ball: bootleg. Did someone lead up into the line? Insert.
- Where was the backside end when the back made his cut? On the ground (cut), chasing (and how close), or
  blocked?
- If the defense has been flowing hard all game, start watching for the bootleg off the same look.

For your prediction log ([01-06](../01-foundations/01-06-how-to-watch-a-broadcast.qmd)): before each zone run
write I (inside), O (outside) or S (split) from the alignment; afterwards write which of bang, bend or bounce
the back chose.
:::

## Predict the play

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 1.** First-and-10 from your own 40. The offense is in the shotgun with one back and one tight end
([11 personnel](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-01-personnel-groupings.qmd)); the tight end is in-line on the right and the running back is offset to the quarterback's
**left**. The defense is in [nickel](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd) with two deep safeties: six defenders in the box against six blockers.
Its linemen are a 5 and a 1 on the left, and a 3 and a **7-technique** (on the tight end's inside
shoulder) on the right. The offense calls inside zone. Which way is it most likely going, does the front
change that, and why does the defense's picture make a run attractive here?

```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-1
#| fig-cap: "Drill 1: gun, 11 personnel, back offset to the quarterback's left, tight end in-line on the right; nickel defense (NB is the nickel back) with two deep safeties and six in the box. The 7 is a 7-technique, on the tight end's inside shoulder."
off = named_line(offense("gun_2x2"))
off = [q.moved(d=-0.7, w=4.8) if q.key == "Y" else (q.moved(w=-2.0) if q.key == "RB" else
       (q.moved(d=-1.5) if q.key == "Z" else q)) for q in off]          # Z off the ball: 7 on the line
from gridiron import defense
DL_TECH = {"SDE": "7", "SDT": "3", "WDT": "1", "WDE": "5"}
dfn = []
for q in defense("nickel", "two_high", off):
    if q.key == "NB":
        q = q.moved(d=5.0, w=-8.5, label="NB")
    elif q.key in DL_TECH:
        q = q.moved(label=DL_TECH[q.key])
    elif q.pos == "CB":
        q = q.moved(label="CB")
    dfn.append(q)
p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=10, title="Drill 1: 1st and 10, gun, 11 personnel")
f = draw(p, lateral=(-17.5, 17.5), window=(-8, 13))
say(f, p, -6.9, -5.6, "RB offset to\nthe QB's left", fontsize=7)
plt.show()
```

::: {.content-visible unless-format="typst"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Most likely to the right, toward the tight end.** From the shotgun, inside zone usually has the back cross
the quarterback's face: he lines up on one side and runs to the other, which gives him a running start toward
the aiming point and a downhill angle at the mesh. With the tight end on the right too, the right side is
also where the offense has its extra blocker.

**Does the front change it?** Not the direction. Run the rules to the right: the RG is covered by the 3 and
the RT by the 7, so the RG has no uncovered neighbor to help him and the 3-technique is the hardest block on
the play side. That tells you where trouble is likely (a 3 who wins knocks the back off his track, and he
bends), not which way the play is called. The back's alignment is the stronger tell.

**Why run here:** two deep safeties and six in the box means six blockers for six defenders: "hat on a hat," a
fair fight up front, with both safeties starting 11–12 yards away. That is exactly the look zone teams want to
run against, and it is a common look now: [two-high](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd)
shells rose from about a third of snaps in 2018 to 42% in 2025.[^twohigh]

**The catch:** good defenses know the "cross the face" tendency too, which is why offenses mix in same-side
zone and the pistol. If you see a team do that a lot, that is why.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 2.** Outside zone to the right is called. The play-side end (on the offense's right) is lined up
*wide*, outside the tight end in a 9-technique, and the Sam linebacker lines up off the ball behind the right
tackle. Before the snap, use the rules: who blocks the 9, who blocks the Sam, and where is the crease most
likely to be? Which of bounce, bang or bend does that make the favorite?

```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-2
#| fig-cap: "Drill 2: outside zone right (the back's track to the aiming point is shown), against a play-side end aligned wide in a 9-technique."
dfn = even_front(+1, cb_w=10.0)
dfn = [q.moved(w=6.0, label="9") if q.key == "PE" else q for q in dfn]
dfn = [q.moved(d=4.5, w=3.4) if q.key == "SAM" else (q.moved(w=1.0) if q.key == "MIKE" else q) for q in dfn]
p = Play(ace_condensed(), dfn, los=40, to_go=10, title="Drill 2: outside zone right is called")
go_to(p, "RB", (-1.3, 4.9), "run", via=[(-4.3, 2.6)])
f = draw(p, width_in=5.4, lateral=(-12, 12), window=(-8, 12.5))
spot(f, p, -0.2, 5.3)
say(f, p, 2.9, 8.6, "end aligned\nwide (9-tech)", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
plt.show()
```

::: {.content-visible unless-format="typst"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Most likely bang, inside the end.** Run the rules. The tight end is covered by a man lined up *outside* him,
the edge case with no help: he has to block the 9 alone, and reaching him (getting the tight end's head across
his outside shoulder) is close to impossible, so his job becomes "ride him wider." The right tackle now has
nobody on him and nobody in his play-side gap: uncovered. His backside neighbor, the right guard, is uncovered
too (the 1 sits in the center's play-side gap, so the RG helps the center), so the right tackle has nobody to
double and climbs straight to the Sam stacked behind him. The back's first read is the end: he will not be
pinned inside, so bounce is off. But a wide end riding wider stretches the gap inside him, so the crease is
likely to appear between the tight end and the tackle, in the Sam's gap. If the right tackle gets to the Sam,
bang.

**What would make it bend:** that is the second read. If the Sam beats the right tackle into that gap, or the
Mike scrapes hard over the top to fill it, the back's third answer is the cutback. A wide 9-technique is a defense
saying "we will not let you have the edge"; outside zone's answer is to stop trying for it and take what the
alignment gives.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 3.** Third time this drive: the offense lines up in the same two-tight-end set it has run outside zone
right from twice already. Both times the backside end (on the offense's left) beat the U's cut-off by
crashing hard inside him at the snap, then flattened down the line and chased the back from behind (the orange
arrow shows what he did; the faint dashed line is the back's track on those runs). It is second-and-6. What call
punishes him?

```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-3
#| fig-cap: "Drill 3: the same two-tight-end look for the third time. The orange arrow shows what the backside (left) end did on the last two outside zone runs: crash inside the U at the snap, then flatten behind the line, chasing the back's track (faint dashes)."
p = Play(ace_condensed(), even_front(+1, cb_w=10.0), los=40, to_go=6,
         title="Drill 3: the same look, third time this drive")
go_to(p, "BE", (-3.0, 1.4), "path", via=[(0.3, -4.0), (-1.3, -3.9), (-2.5, -1.6)])
f = draw(p, width_in=5.4, lateral=(-12, 12), window=(-8, 12.5))
branch(f, p, [(-7.0, 0.0), (-4.3, 2.6), (-1.3, 4.9), (1.5, 5.6)], color=style.MUTED, lw=1.3, dash=(0, (2, 2.5)))
say(f, p, -3.4, -7.2, "what this end did on\nthe last two zone runs", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
plt.show()
```

::: {.content-visible unless-format="typst"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**A bootleg the other way (left), probably naked.** An end who crashes hard on every outside-zone fake is the
exact defender the bootleg is built to beat: the quarterback fakes outside zone right, the end chases the fake,
and the quarterback rolls left behind him with the flat open and a crosser coming across. The end has been
beating the U's cut-off anyway, so the boot turns his speed into a liability: the harder he crashes, the farther
behind the quarterback he ends up. Second-and-6 is a
comfortable down for it, too: even a short completion in the flat keeps the offense on schedule.

**A second good answer:** split zone, with a tight end kicking out that end. If the end is going to
crash, block him and let the back cut back behind him. Coaches choose between the two by asking whether they want
to *punish* the end (the boot, for a potential big play) or *neutralize* him (split zone, for a safer run). Either
way, his habit has become information, and that is how a zone offense talks to itself across a drive.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 4.** This one is *after* the snap. Shotgun, back offset to the quarterback's left, an H-back off the
ball on the left. @fig-predict-4 shows the first second: everyone's first steps and paths. Inside or outside
zone? Which tag is this? What is the quarterback looking at, and what does he do if that man chases the back?

```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-4
#| fig-cap: "Drill 4: the first second after the snap. Lines ending in a bar are blocks (look at the direction of each lineman's first step); the dashed line from the quarterback shows where his eyes are."
off = [q for q in named_line(offense("gun_2x2")) if q.key in (*OL_NAMES, "QB", "Y", "Z", "X")]
off = [q.moved(d=-0.7, w=4.8) if q.key == "Y" else (q.moved(d=-1.5) if q.key == "Z" else q) for q in off]
off += [Player("H", "TE", "off", -1.5, -6.6, label="H"), Player("RB", "RB", "off", -5.0, -1.6, label="R")]
dfn = [q for q in front7() if q.key != "SAM"] + [D("SS", "SS", 5.0, -9.6, "SS"), D("NB", "NB", 4.5, 8.0, "NB")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=10, title="Drill 4: name the play and the tag")
p.block("C", pts=[(0.9, 0.5)]); p.block("RG", pts=[(0.8, -0.8), (4.3, -0.4)])
p.block("RT", pts=[(0.9, 0.6)]); p.block("Y", pts=[(0.6, -0.6), (3.6, 1.5)])
p.block("LT", pts=[(0.9, 0.7)]); p.block("LG", pts=[(0.8, -0.6), (4.3, -0.8)])
go_to(p, "H", (4.1, -9.3), via=[(0.4, -7.6), (2.6, -9.0)])
go_to(p, "RB", (-1.4, 2.3), "run", via=[(-4.0, -0.4)])
p.read("BE")
f = draw(p, width_in=5.6, lateral=(-12.5, 11), window=(-8, 9))
plt.show()
```

::: {.content-visible unless-format="typst"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Inside zone right, with an arc tag.** The linemen's first steps go *up*, not across, and the back is
crossing the quarterback's face toward the right B gap: inside zone. The H runs past the backside end without
touching him and heads for the safety outside him: that is an arc block, not split zone (he would hit the end)
and not a bootleg (he would turn into the flat and look for the ball). The quarterback is reading the unblocked
backside end. If the end stays home, he hands off. If the end chases the back down the line, he pulls the ball
and runs around the end, behind the H's block on the safety.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="typst"}
*The answers to the four drills are at the end of the chapter, after Connections.*
:::

## Takeaways

- Zone blocking assigns blockers by **rule, not by name**: step play-side; block the man head-up on you or in
  your play-side gap; if nobody is, help the neighbor on your backside and climb to a linebacker. Because the
  rules are applied after the snap, slants and blitzes get picked up, and the same call re-pairs itself
  against every front.
- **Inside zone** attacks the guard-tackle area with double teams that drive defenders backward; **outside
  (wide) zone** aims at the tight end's outside leg and moves the defense sideways with reach-and-overtake
  blocks; **stretch** is the widest track, edge first; **split zone** adds a crossing H to kick the backside end.
  Tell them apart by the line's first step (up or across) and the back's aiming point.
- The running back makes the play's last decision: **press the aiming point, then bang, bend or bounce**, with
  one cut. On inside zone the order is bang-bend-bounce; on outside zone it is bounce-bang-bend.
- The **cutback** is designed, not improvised: it works because the defense over-runs the play and the
  **backside cut-off** keeps the backside defenders out of the lane (in Gibbs's Denver, often with a cut block,
  a legal but controversial low block that the rules have steadily narrowed).
- Tags change one or two jobs to fix one problem: **insert** adds a lead blocker, **arc** runs past the unblocked
  end to block the next man while the quarterback reads the end, **bash** sends the back away and makes the
  quarterback the inside runner. Defenses fight
  back with penetration, a cutback player and coordinated run fits.
- Outside zone's biggest payoff is the **bootleg** that looks identical for the first second. The data shows zone
  running is efficient for a run game, not magic; its value is in what it sets up.

::: {.callout-note title="Go deeper"}
**Names you will hear.** Zone vocabulary is a dialect map. Alex Gibbs called inside zone **tight zone**, and many coaches still do. Some analysts describe
a **mid zone** between inside and outside zone, in which the play-side tackle pushes the end outward
instead of trying to reach him, so the back's read moves to the defensive tackles; one coach-analyst
used the name for Sean McVay's Rams' base run.[^names] Split zone is also called **zone slice**,
and bash is sometimes spelled out as **back away**. And **duo**, a two-back or one-back run with double
teams that a casual viewer can mistake for inside zone, is not a zone play at all: the linemen do not
take zone steps and the back reads a linebacker. It belongs to the gap family in
[03-03](03-03-gap-and-power-runs.qmd).
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Go deeper"}
**From diagrams to real tracking data.** Every animation in this chapter is a gridiron simulation written
in NFL Big Data Bowl (BDB) coordinates, the format of the league's public tracking-data competition, so real
tracking data drops into the same drawing code. The 2025 Big Data Bowl release (2022 season, weeks 1–9)
includes pre-snap and post-snap frames for every player, and its `plays.csv` carries a run-concept label
from PFF, so you can pull real outside-zone runs and watch the line step together. The data is hosted on
Kaggle (a data-science competition site) and needs your own free login, so the code for this (in the web
edition of this chapter, under "Show the Python") is not run when this book is built.

```{python}
#| eval: false
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (real Big Data Bowl tracking; not run in the build)"
import pandas as pd
from gridiron import bdb, show_animation

plays = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/plays.csv")
oz = plays[plays["pff_runConceptPrimary"].astype(str).str.upper().str.contains("OUTSIDE ZONE")]
print(len(oz), "outside zone runs")
g, pl = oz.iloc[0][["gameId", "playId"]]

trk = bdb.load_tracking("data/bdb/tracking_week_*.csv")
one = bdb.prepare(trk, plays, game_id=g, play_id=pl)
show_animation(one, times=[0.0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.6])   # same call as the simulated plays
```
:::

## Drill answers

**Drill 1. Most likely to the right, toward the tight end.** From the shotgun, inside zone usually has the back
cross the quarterback's face: he lines up on one side and runs to the other, which gives him a running start
toward the aiming point and a downhill angle at the mesh. With the tight end on the right too, the right side is
also where the offense has its extra blocker. *Does the front change it?* Not the direction. By the rules the
RG is covered by the 3 and the RT by the 7, so the RG has no help and the 3 is the hardest play-side block; that
tells you where trouble is likely (a 3 who wins makes the back bend), not which way the play is called.
*Why run here:* two deep safeties and six in the box means six blockers for six defenders: "hat on a hat," a fair
fight up front, with both safeties starting 11–12 yards away. That is the look zone teams want to run against,
and a common one now: two-high shells rose from about a third of snaps in 2018 to 42% in 2025.[^twohigh] *The catch:* good defenses know the "cross the face" tendency too, which is why offenses mix
in same-side zone and the pistol.

**Drill 2. Most likely bang, inside the end.** Run the rules. The tight end is covered by a man lined up
*outside* him, with no help, so he cannot reach him; his job becomes "ride him wider." The right tackle is
uncovered, and so is the right guard beside him (the guard helps the center on the 1), so the tackle has nobody
to double and climbs straight to the Sam. The back's first read is the end: he will not be pinned inside, so
bounce is off. A wide end riding wider stretches the gap inside him, so the crease is likely between the tight
end and the tackle, in the Sam's gap: if the tackle gets to the Sam, bang. *What would make it bend:* the second
read. If the Sam beats the tackle into that gap, or the Mike scrapes over the top to fill it, the back's third
answer is the cutback. A wide 9-technique says "we will not let you have the edge";
outside zone's answer is to stop trying for it and take what the alignment gives.

**Drill 3. A bootleg the other way (left), probably naked.** An end who crashes hard on every outside-zone fake is
the exact defender the bootleg is built to beat: the quarterback fakes outside zone right, the end chases the
fake, and the quarterback rolls left behind him with the flat open and a crosser coming across. He has been
beating the U's cut-off anyway; the boot turns that speed into a liability. Second-and-6 is a
comfortable down for it: even a short completion in the flat keeps the offense on schedule. *A second good
answer:* split zone, with a tight end kicking out that end. Coaches choose between the two by asking whether they
want to *punish* the end (the boot) or *neutralize* him (split zone). Either way, his habit has become
information, and that is how a zone offense talks to itself across a drive.

**Drill 4. Inside zone right, with an arc tag.** The linemen's first steps go *up*, not across, and the back is
crossing the quarterback's face toward the right B gap: inside zone. The H runs past the backside end without
touching him and heads for the safety outside him: an arc block, not split zone (he would hit the end) and not a
bootleg (he would turn into the flat and look for the ball). The quarterback is reading the unblocked backside
end: if the end stays home, he hands off; if the end chases the back, he keeps and runs around the end, behind
the H's block on the safety.
:::

    coaches' survey, 42.1% taught linemen to come off the double team when they see the linebacker work underneath
    or over the top of it, and 35.7% when the linebacker reaches the blocker's level. The same article covers naming
    the combination blocks and how terminology varies by staff (one system calls the tight end-tackle,
    tackle-guard and center-guard pairs "Ted," "Tag" and "Cage").

    ("Because of the technique the Rams employ with their play-side tackle, I refer to this scheme as a
    'mid-zone' play"): <https://ramstalk.net/overview-of-the-los-angeles-rams-offense/>. "Zone slice": Jon Svec,
    "Defending Split Zone," Jan 12, 2022: <https://jonsvec.substack.com/p/defending-split-zone>.

[^bbb]: Chris B. Brown, *The Art of Smart Football* (2015), and his Smart Football posts on the inside zone

    <https://grantland.com/features/chris-brown-gary-kubiak-houston-texans-running-game/>.

    Peel-back blocks banned everywhere (2013) and all chop blocks banned (2016): NFL, "Health and safety-related rules

[^bash]: "Bash" = "back away": the back runs away from the line's zone flow and the quarterback becomes the inside

    the exact read vary by team.
